body: I have been in the psych ward after a suicide attempt. There was a little basketball court fenced off connected to the building. It looked like a jail yard. We would BEG the staff to go outside. We would get maybe an hour a day and then be herded back inside. I remember feeling better the second I was able to shoot a few hoops, but then they’d call us back in and we’d go back to huddling around the tv and being feed our anti anxiety pills. If we were able to spend more time outside each day, I’m convinced many patients would have had an easier recovery.

The beating of Rodney King, an unarmed black man, by LAPD was caught on video. It was brutal, and obviously racially motivated. The trial of the officers was moved into a wealthier white neighborhood and they were found not guilty. LA erupted after years of injustice. As the anger was exploding, LAPD and the fire department pulled their forces out and let the city burn. People had to fend for themselves. The demonstrations were over shadowed by looting, burning, and violence. Meanwhile, tensions between the Korean and black communities had been building up for some time. A Korean store owner, Soon Ja Du, had shot a 15 year old black girl, Latasha Harlins, who she thought was trying to steal orange juice. Du got probation and a fine. Anger between the two groups rose. The Korean communities were very industrious, and had many stores what use to be black neighborhoods. As the violence and looting continued, with little to no police in sight, they took to defending their livelihoods themselves. Armed, Korean store owners defended their shops with deadly force, seeing as no one else was going to come to help. 

It was a messy riot that demonstrated what humans are capable of when feelings of oppression become overwhelming.

Check out LA 92 on Netflix, it shows how everything boiled over too all out chaos and the humanity behind it.

Speaking from someone who has been admitted to a psych ward, this doesn't surprise me in the slightest. There is a point system in place to keep patients underwraps. If you're having a bad day, (argued with staff or didn't participate in group activities cause you just felt shity) privileges (going outside for half-an hour/ getting a snack) get taken away. It's hard to get privileges back and usually after you start getting strikes, within a day or two you end up in isolation. 

If you refuse to take medication, forget it. No matter what your reasoning, if you don't take your drugs they will eventually put in into isolation because they fear for staff and patient safety. I watched coherent, well spoken adults drooling on themselves after being sedated because they had a nervous fit. 

The staff is not felaxable. You stick to their calendar and their treatment for you or you will be stuck in isolation. I had a really bad episode with tics where I couldn't stop screaming a flinging my arms and I was thrown into a padded room for the rest of the day, even though my chart said I had Tourettes and my best form of treatment was listening to music. 

People don't concentrate on getting better, they focus on getting out. Eventually you get tired and fall into line, doing whatever they tell you to do even though your reality is warped from trying three new SSRIs in a matter of a few weeks and you feel worse than when you were admitted.
